sec.title: Background
sec.p: Currently, an epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII)-specific peptide (PEPvIII) vaccine has not achieved satisfactory outcomes in several clinical trials for glioblastoma. This is probably due to the poor immunogenicity of the PEPvIII peptide vaccine and the harshly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Hence, identifying strategies to enhance tumor-specific T cell immune responses and reverse immune suppression is crucial for achieving the maximum beneficial therapeutic effect.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: To enhance the immunogenicity of the PEPvIII vaccine, we have developed a novel oncolytic adenovirus-based vaccine by genetically incorporating the PEPvIII peptide into the adenovirus hexon protein, naming this construct Ad5-D24-PEPvIII. However, the upregulation of programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in the tumor microenvironment following oncolytic virus therapy may limit its therapeutic effectiveness. To address this, we first attempted to co-express soluble programmed cell death 1 (sPD-1) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) in the E4 region of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII. Subsequently, we combined the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine carrying GM-CSF with a PD-L1 inhibitor. Two immunocompetent mouse glioma models were used to evaluate their antitumor effects in vivo. The immune cell status within the tumor microenvironment was assessed using flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry. CD8+ T cell immune responses were evaluated by ELISA.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Local administration of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, which presents high copies of tumor-specific antigen PEPvIII in the hexon protein, successfully activated PEPvIII-specific T cell responses. Co-expression of sPD-1 and GM-CSF in the E4 region of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII could increase the release of proinflammatory cytokines, activate myeloid cells and promote the maturation of dendritic cells, thereby further enhancing the activation and proliferation of CD8+ T cells targeting tumor antigens. More importantly, when the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine carrying GM-CSF was combined with a PD-L1 inhibitor, it could also broaden the tumor antigenic epitopes and significantly inhibit tumor growth in immunocompetent glioma mouse models.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our work suggests that the efficient presentation of PEPvIII, achieved by modifying the hexon protein of the oncolytic adenovirus, combined with the adjuvant function of GM-CSF and blockade of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, significantly enhances the therapeutic efficacy of the PEPvIII vaccine against glioblastoma. In addition, this combination strategy also provides a promising and personalized treatment for patients with cancer.

caption.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: The novel PEPvIII vaccine based on oncolytic adenovirus, which was achieved by modifying the hexon protein with PEPvIII, is capable of inducing PEPvIII-specific T cell immune responses.

The oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine, when combined with the adjuvant function of granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and blockade of the programmed cell death 1/programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) axis, can overcome the limitations of traditional vaccines by remodeling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and enhancing T cell immune responses to tumor antigens and tumor neoantigens.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: This study demonstrates that the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine, which enhances PEPvIII-specific T cell responses through the synergistic action of GM-CSF and blockade of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, effectively suppresses the growth of gliomas and warrants further testing of the novel vaccine in clinical trials.

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant tumor of the central nervous system in adults, hard to remove completely by surgery and prone to recurrence.1 Despite aggressive treatments, the median overall survival of patients is still less than 15 months.2 Epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (EGFRvIII) is a tumor-specific receptor expressed only on the surface of tumor cells. It has an in-frame deletion of 801 base pairs, resulting in the deletion of amino acids 6–273 in the extracellular domain and generation of a 13-amino acid peptide (LEEKKGNYVVTDH), termed PEPvIII.3 4 PEPvIII conjugated to keyhole limpet hemocyanin has been used to vaccinate humans with EGFRvIII-expressing GBM.5 Regrettably, in clinical trials for newly diagnosed GBM, it did not achieve satisfactory results.6 These findings suggest that vaccines targeting EGFRvIII should be further optimized to improve vaccine-based immunotherapy.

In recent years, oncolytic viruses have received considerable attention in tumor therapy because of their ability to specifically lyse tumor cells and induce a strong immune response.7 8 However, current oncolytic virus-based vaccines mainly induce antiviral immunity, rather than antitumor immunity, probably due to the lower loading and weaker immunogenicity of tumor antigens compared with viral antigens. Thus, to enhance the immunogenicity of tumor antigens, the PEPvIII can be inserted into the hexon protein, which is a capsid protein with hundreds of copies per virion.9 This strategy markedly improved the copies of PEPvIII and enhanced the immunogenicity of PEPvIII by the peptide-modified oncolytic adenovirus.

Programmed cell death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), a ligand for PD-1, is commonly expressed in tumor cells and immune cells. Infection of tumor cells with an oncolytic virus leads to the expression of PD-L1 in the tumor microenvironment (TME), which interacts with PD-1 on the surface of T cells to inhibit T cell function, potentially resulting in drug resistance.10 Therefore, many studies have attempted to use oncolytic viruses to deliver immune checkpoint inhibitors, immune costimulatory molecules, and chemokines to remodel the TME.11 12 Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) exerts antitumor activity by enhancing dendritic cell (DC) activation and antigen presentation and improving T cell function.13 14 Soluble PD-1 (sPD-1), the extracellular domain of PD-1, can be used as an immune checkpoint inhibitor to block the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway, thereby activating specific CD8+ T cell immune responses; sPD-1 thus has an immune-enhancing adjuvant effect.15 16

In this study, we generated a novel oncolytic adenovirus vaccine by modifying the second-generation oncolytic virus Delta-24-RGD, a conditionally replicating adenovirus capable of replicating in retinoblastoma protein-deficient cells.17 18 A novel oncolytic adenovirus vaccine with PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, was found to effectively induce T cell responses against tumor antigens. However, it also induced PD-L1 expression in the TME, potentially limiting its therapeutic efficacy. We employed two strategies to reduce the immunosuppression mediated by the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. First, we co-expressed GM-CSF and sPD-1 in the E4 region of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, resulting in an “all-in-one” oncolytic adenovirus vaccine, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF. Subsequently, we employed a second strategy by combining the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine carrying GM-CSF with a PD-L1 inhibitor. These two strategies exhibited superior antitumor activity in two immunocompetent glioma mouse models by promoting DC maturation, remodeling the immunosuppressive TME, and further enhancing the activation and proliferation of tumor antigen-specific T cells. These findings provide an effective strategy to improve the immunogenicity and therapeutic efficacy of peptide-based cancer vaccines.

sec.title: Cell lines and cell culture
sec.p: The human malignant glioma cell lines U87 MG and U251, the human embryonic kidney cell line HEK293, and the mouse malignant glioma cell lines GL261 and CT-2A were purchased from American Type Culture Collection. GL261 glioma cells and CT-2A glioma cells co-expressed with the mouse EGFRvIII gene and firefly luciferase gene (termed GL261/EGFRvIII and CT-2A/EGFRvIII, respectively) were prepared by transfection with the lentiviral vector system retained in Xia’s laboratory. All cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco, Carlsbad, California, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Sijiqing, Hangzhou, China), 100 U/mL penicillin, 100 µg/mL streptomycin, and 200 µg/mL L-glutamine, and were incubated in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 at 37°C.

sec.title: Plasmid construction and preparation of recombinant oncolytic adenovirus
sec.p: Following a previously reported methodology,19,21 the PEPvIII modification in hexon protein and the E4 region co-expressing murine GM-CSF and murine sPD-1 in adenoviral vectors were constructed by following these steps: (1) The forward primer and reverse primer of the chemically synthesized BglII-PEPvIII-ClaI DNA sequence, each at 5 µL, were annealed and extended for 2.5 hours at room temperature to form the BglII-PEPvIII-ClaI linker. The linker was ligated into the pAd5-D24-HVR5-LacZ-SV40pA oncolytic adenovirus backbone vector digested by BamHI and SfuI (kept in Xia’s laboratory); the obtained plasmid was named pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-SV40pA. (2) The pAd5-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-PGK-miniCMV-MCS shuttle vector, preserved in Xia’s laboratory, was linearized by PacI digestion and co-transformed with the SwaI-digested pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-SV40pA adenoviral backbone vector into Escherichia coli strain Bj5183 for homologous recombination. The resulting plasmid was named pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-Fiber-RGD. (3) The target mouse gene GM-CSF and mouse extracellular domain PD-1 were cloned into the E4 shuttle vector pAd5-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-PGK-miniCMV-MCS containing a bidirectional promoter to express eGFP and the target genes. The adenoviral E4 shuttle vectors were obtained and named: pShuttle-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA and pShuttle-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-T2A-sPD-1-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA, respectively. (4) The PacI-linearized pShuttle-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA vector was co-transformed with the SwaI-digested pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-SV40pA adenoviral backbone vector into E. coli strain Bj5183 for homologous recombination. The obtained plasmid was named pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA. Similarly, the PacI-linearized pShuttle-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-T2A-sPD-1-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA vector was co-transformed with the SwaI-digested pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-SV40pA adenoviral backbone vector into E. coli strain Bj5183 for homologous recombination, and the obtained plasmid was named pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-T2A-sPD-1-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA. Using a similar strategy, we constructed a control adenovirus lacking PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein but co-expressing murine GM-CSF and sPD-1 in the E4 region, and the obtained plasmid was named pAd5-D24-HVR5-Fiber-RGD-eGFP-T2A-sPD-1-PGK-miniCMV-mGM-CSF-SV40pA. As previously reported, the adenovirus vectors were linearized using PacI and then transfected into HEK293 cells separately.22 Subsequently, adenovirus production and amplification were observed. Finally, the virus was purified, dialysis was performed, and titers were determined. The final recombinant oncolytic adenoviruses were named Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF, and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF.

sec.title: RNA extraction and real-time PCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from mouse GBMs injected with oncolytic adenoviruses and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) using a HiPure Universal RNA kit (Magen, Guangzhou, Guangdong, China). RNA samples were quantified using a Nanodrop One spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA) and stored at −80°C. cDNA synthesis was performed using the Prime Script RT Reagent Kit (TaKaRa, Dalian, Liaoning, China) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Real-time PCR was performed on an ABI 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, California, USA) using a SYBR green PCR Kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany). The target genes were adenovirus E4 and Hexon, with GAPDH (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) serving as the housekeeping gene. All samples were run in triplicate. The mean value calculated by the 2−ΔΔCT method was used to calculate the fold change of the target gene expression. The primer sequences are shown in table 1.

sec.title: Cell viability assay
sec.p: U87 MG, U251, GL261, and CT-2A cells were seeded in 96-well plates (5×103 cells/well), with each cell line being seeded separately. The following day, different oncolytic adenoviruses infected the above tumor cells at 1 multiplicity of infection (MOI), 5 MOIs, 25 MOIs, and 50 MOIs. At 24, 48, and 72 hours after infection, cell viability was detected by 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)−2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide assay. The survival ratio (%) was calculated according to the following formula: (experimental group absorbance − background absorbance)/(control group absorbance − background absorbance) × 100%.

sec.title: Detection of PD-L1 expression on tumor cells in vitro
sec.p: Mouse glioma GL261 cells were inoculated in 6-well plates at 5×105 cells/well. After 48 hours of infection with different oncolytic adenoviruses at 5 MOIs, the cells were collected and the expression of PD-L1 on the cell surface was detected by flow cytometry. For cytokine treatment, tumor cells were treated with 20 ng/mL interferon (IFN)-γ (315–05, PeproTech, Cranbury, New Jersey, USA) for 24 hours to enhance the expression of PD-L1. Tumor cells treated with IFN-γ were then infected with different oncolytic adenoviruses for 48 hours and stained with anti-PD-L1. The staining results were analyzed by flow cytometry.

sec.title: ELISA
sec.p: After the indicated oncolytic adenoviruses had infected tumor cells at 20 MOIs for 72 hours, tumor cell culture supernatants were collected. The concentrations of sPD-1 and GM-CSF were determined using a mouse PD-1 ELISA kit (NeoBioscience, Shenzhen, China) or a mouse GM-CSF ELISA kit (NeoBioscience, Shenzhen, China).

sec.title: Animal studies
sec.p: All procedures involving animals were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Shaanxi Normal University, China. C57BL/6 mice, 6–8 weeks old, were purchased from the Shaanxi Normal University Laboratory Animal Centre. The mice were maintained in a controlled environment (12/12 hours light/dark cycle, 23±1°C, 55±10% humidity) and given free access to food and water. GL261/EGFRvIII cells (5×104 cells) or CT-2A/EGFRvIII cells (5×104 cells) were resuspended in 5 µL of PBS and stereotactically implanted into the right striatum (2 mm lateral, 1 mm anterior to Bregma, depth 3 mm) on day 0 to generate intracranial tumors. The mice were randomly divided into groups, with each group comprising 10 mice. On day 7 post-implantation, the establishment of tumors was confirmed using bioluminescence imaging and intratumorally injected with different oncolytic adenoviruses (5×107 plaque-forming units (PFU)/mouse) or 5 µL of PBS as a control on days 7, 9, and 11. For the GL261/EGFRvIII model, tumor progression was monitored using bioluminescence imaging on days 14, 21, and 28 after tumor cell implantation. For the CT-2A/EGFRvIII model, tumor progression was monitored using bioluminescence imaging on days 12, 17, and 22 after tumor cell implantation.

To evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of oncolytic adenovirus and PD-L1 blockade, GL261/EGFRvIII cells or CT-2A/EGFRvIII cells were implanted according to the above method. Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF (5×107 PFU/mouse) was intratumorally (i.t.) injected three times on days 7, 9, and 11 (three injections total) after tumor cell implantation. The PD-L1 antibody (200 µg/injection; clone 10F.9G2, #BE0101, Bio X Cell) was injected intraperitoneally on days 9, 12, 15, and 18 after tumor cell implantation. The experimental and testing sequences for all mice were randomly assigned. The animal care staff was unaware of the allocation groups. Mice were monitored daily to assess mortality and survival, and if neurological deficits and weight loss were observed, the mice were euthanized.

sec.title: Flow cytometry and cell separation
sec.p: Tumors were excised from the brains of tumor-bearing mice and washed with PBS on day 7 after the last oncolytic adenovirus treatment, unless otherwise specified. The tumors were then minced, digested with 0.66 mg/mL Collagenase D and 8 U/mL DNase I (both from Roche, Basel, Switzerland) in serum-free Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium for 30 min at 37°C, and then filtered through a 70 µm nylon filter (Corning, New York, USA) to obtain a single-cell suspension. Immune cells were separated by gradient centrifugation with 30% and 70% Percoll (GE Healthcare, 17-0891-02, DE, USA). Cell precipitates were collected and washed twice with a complete RPMI 1640 medium and stained with antibodies specific for antigenic markers. Cell surface antigens were stained using the following antibodies: mouse CD45 PerCP-Cy5.5 (clone: 30-F11, BioLegend, #103132), mouse CD3 FITC (clone: 17A2, BioLegend, #100204), mouse CD4 APC (clone: RM4-5, eBioscience, #17-0042-82), mouse CD8a APC/Cy7 (clone: 53–6.7, BioLegend, #100708), CD11b APC/Cy7 (clone: M1-70, BioLegend, #101226), mouse CD11c APC or FITC (clone: N418, BioLegend, #117 309 or #117305), mouse MHCII PerCP-eFluor 710 (clone: M5/114.15.2, eBioscience, #46-5321-82), mouse CD86 PE (clone: GL-1, eBioscience, #12-0862-82), mouse F4/80 PE-Cy7 (clone: BM8, eBioscience, #25-4801-82), mouse Gr-1 APC (clone: RB6-8C5, BioLegend, #108411), mouse PD-L1 APC or PE (clone: 10F.9G2, BioLegend, #124311, #124307), mouse PD-1 PE/Dazzle 594 or PE (clone: 29F.1A12, BioLegend, #135227, #135205), mouse TIM-3 PE (clone: RMT3-23, eBioscience, #12-5870-81), and NK 1.1 PE (clone: PK136, BioLegend, #108707). For intracellular staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized with Fixation and Permeabilization Solution (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, New Jersey, USA); washed three times; and stained with the following antibodies: mouse IFN-γ PE-eFluor 610 (clone: XMG1.2, eBioscience, #61-7311-82), mouse TNF-α PE-Cy7 (clone: MP6-XT22, eBioscience, #25-7321-80), mouse IL-12 PE (clone: 27537,eBioscience, #MA5-23559), mouse IL-10 APC (clone: JES5-16E3, BioLegend, #505009), and mouse Foxp3 PE (clone: FJK-16s, eBioscience, #12-5773-80). Samples were collected on a Beckman Coulter CytoFLEX S instrument, and data were analyzed with FlowJo software.

sec.title: Isolation of spleen and tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and bone marrow-derived dendritic cells
sec.p: Mouse spleen cells were isolated, placed on a 100 µm cell strainer, and filtered into a centrifuge tube. Cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 medium and centrifuged at 350×g for 7 min at room temperature, then resuspended in Red Blood Cell Lysis Buffer (Solarbio, Beijing, China) to lyse the red blood cells. Splenocytes are obtained after centrifugation again. Tumor-infiltrating immune cells were collected by density gradient centrifugation. Then, the CD8+ T cells from the harvested splenocytes and tumor-infiltrating immune cells were isolated using a Mouse CD8a+ T Cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany).

Monocytes were isolated from the bone marrow of the femurs and tibias of the syngeneic mice. Subsequently, the monocytes were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, recombinant mouse GM-CSF (20 ng/mL, PeproTech, Cranbury, New Jersey, USA), and recombinant mouse interleukin (IL)-4 (20 ng/mL, PeproTech, Cranbury, New Jersey, USA) for 7 days. The non-adherent cells, that is, the bone marrow-derived dendritic cells, were treated with 1 µg/mL lipopolysaccharide (Sigma-Aldrich, Saint Louis, Missouri, USA) for an additional 18 hours to induce dendritic cell maturation.

sec.title: Antigen-stimulated CD8+ T cells
sec.p: To prepare target cells, mouse primary astrocytes, GL261 cells, GL261/EGFRvIII cells, CT-2A cells, and CT-2A/EGFRvIII cells were inoculated in round-bottom 96-well plates at 2×104 cells/well. GL261 cells, Gl261/EGFRvIII cells, CT-2A cells, and CT-2A/EGFRvIII cells were treated with 20 ng/mL IFN-γ for 24 hours. To activate CD8+ T cells, splenic CD8+ T cells (4×105 cells/well) or tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (2×105 cells/well) were incubated with target cells. To assess the PEPvIII-specific T cell responses, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (3×105 cells/well) were stimulated with bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (1×105 cells /well) that had been pulsed overnight with the PEPvIII peptide (100 µg/mL). 40 hours after co-culture in a round-bottom 96-well plate, the concentration of IFN-γ in the supernatant was assessed by ELISA (Mouse IFN-γ DuoSet, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA).

sec.title: Cell proliferation assay
sec.p: Tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells were isolated from mice treated with different oncolytic adenoviruses and labeled with 5 µM carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE, Solarbio, Beijing, China) at 37°C for 10 min. After removing excess dye with complete medium, the labeled CD8+ T cells (5×105 cells/well) were co-cultured with dendritic cells (5×104 cells/well) pulsed with PEPvIII peptide for 4 days. The fluorescence decay of the CFSE-stained T cells was detected and analyzed by flow cytometry.

sec.title: Neoantigen-specific T cell response assays
sec.p: Tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells (3×105 cells/well) in the different treatment groups were stimulated with different concentrations of GARC-1 peptide-pulsed bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (1×105 cells/well). After 40 hours of co-culture in 96-well plates, the concentration of IFN-γ in the supernatant was assessed by ELISA (mouse IFN-γ DuoSet, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA).

Splenocytes were isolated from tumor-bearing C57BL/6 mice treated with various oncolytic adenoviruses and were cultured in a round-bottom 96-well plate (5×105 cells/well) in the presence of GARC-1 peptide at different concentrations at 37°C in 5% CO2. After 72 hours of incubation, 200 µL of supernatant was collected from each well to evaluate IFN-γ via ELISA (mouse IFN-γ DuoSet, R&D Systems, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA).

sec.title: Bioluminescence imaging
sec.p: Tumor growth in the animals was monitored via bioluminescence imaging. Mice bearing GL261/EGFRvIII cells or CT-2A/EGFRvIII cells were anesthetized with isoflurane and injected intraperitoneally with D-luciferin (150 mg/kg), and animal imaging was performed using an In vivo imaging system (Caliper Life Sciences, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA). Data were analyzed with Living Image software. Researchers involved in animal monitoring and data analysis were blinded to the treatment assigned to each animal.

sec.title: H&E staining and immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Tumor tissues were collected, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Solarbio, Beijing, China) for 72 hours, and stored at 4°C in 70% ethanol for further processing. Then, the tumor tissue was embedded in paraffin, cut into 5 µm thick sections, and H&E-stained for pathological detection. For immunohistochemistry, after antigen retrieval, blocking endogenous peroxidase, and blocking non-specific binding with a blocking buffer containing 3% bovine serum albumin, the sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with a moderately diluted primary antibody. The primary antibodies used were anti-CD8 (1:100, ABclonal, #A23081), anti-CD68 (1:500, Abcam, #ab125212), and anti-iNOS (1:200, Proteintech, #22 226–1-AP or Abcam, #ab3523). The next day, the sections were washed three times in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBST) for 10 min, incubated with the appropriate secondary antibody (VECTASTAIN ABC Kit, Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, California, USA) for 60 min, and finally stained with 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB) horseradish peroxidase (HRP) substrate (Vector Laboratories, Burlingame, California, USA). The HRP enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of DAB, resulting in a brown precipitate that can be visualized under a microscope. The stained sections were observed under a microscope.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Animal survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival curves and statistically analyzed using Log-Rank test (SPSS, Chicago, Illinois, USA). One-way analysis of variance was applied for comparison of more than two groups (GraphPad Prism V.8). Measured data were expressed as mean±SD. A p value<0.05 was considered significant; p>0.05 indicated no significance (ns: not significant).

sec.title: Oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine promotes T cell activation and induces PEPvIII-specific immune responses
sec.p: According to a previously published paper by Di et al,21 we constructed pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-Fiber-RGD by inserting the PEPvIII peptide into the hexon protein by homologous recombination using Delta-24-RGD as the backbone vector (figure 1A). The obtained oncolytic adenovirus plasmid vector, including the Delta-24-RGD plasmid vector, was digested with PacI and transfected into HEK293 cells, and high-titer recombinant oncolytic adenoviruses were obtained after amplification and purification. The final recombinant oncolytic adenoviruses were named Ad5-D24 and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, respectively. We first evaluated the antitumor activity of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII in glioma cells by cell viability assay. The results showed that the oncolytic adenoviruses induced dose-dependent cell-killing activity and the oncolytic adenovirus vector with PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein did not affect the ability of oncolytic adenoviruses to kill tumor cells (figure 1B and online supplemental figure 1). Next, we examined the expression of adenoviral protein mRNA in the tumor tissues at different time points after Ad5-D24-PEPvIII infection. We observed that transcript levels of adenoviral hexon and E4 in tumor tissues increased over time after viral infection (online supplemental figure 2A,B), suggesting the amplification of the oncolytic adenovirus in tumor tissues. To test whether the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII peptide vaccine is capable of eliciting, expanding, and activating tumor-specific T cells, the i.t. injection of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII was carried out in an orthotopically implanted GL261/EGFRvIII cell syngeneic murine model. 7 days after tumor implantation, Ad5-D24 or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII was injected three times at a dose of 5×107 PFU per mouse; PBS was used as a control (figure 1C). 7 days after the final adenovirus injection, the tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were characterized. Compared with the PBS group, intratumoral injections of both Ad5-D24 and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII increased the percentage of infiltration of cytotoxic T cells (CD45+/CD3+/CD8+), and T helper cells (CD45+/CD3+/CD4+) within the tumor (figure 1D). The expression of IFN-γ and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α in these T cells was significantly increased (figure 1E), suggesting that these infiltrating T cells exhibited improved functionality. To further investigate whether these tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells could elicit specific immune responses against PEPvIII peptide, we co-cultured them with dendritic cells pulsed with PEPvIII peptide and used CFSE to track CD8+ T cell proliferation. As illustrated in figure 1F,G, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells isolated from the Ad5-D24-PEPvIII treatment group exhibited specific proliferation and an increased secretion of IFN-γ in response to the PEPvIII peptide. These data demonstrated that the oncolytic adenovirus vaccine with PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein could effectively trigger PEPvIII-specific T cell responses.

sec.p: While Ad5-D24-PEPvIII can induce T cell immune responses against tumors, tumor cells often employ various mechanisms to evade immune system attacks. One such mechanism involves the inhibition of T cell activity by upregulating the expression of PD-L1 on the surface of the tumor cells. It was previously shown that infecting tumor cells with oncolytic virus leads to upregulated PD-L1 in tumor cells.23 24 Moreover, it has also been reported that oncolytic virus infection induces a proinflammatory response and that the release of cytokines and chemokines, such as IFN, can also cause tumor cells to upregulate PD-L1.25 26 To explore this, we therefore compared the expression of PD-L1 on the surface of GL261 cells after oncolytic adenovirus infection and IFN-γ stimulation in vitro. We found that, compared with the PBS group, infection of GL261 cells with oncolytic adenoviruses resulted in a slight upregulation of PD-L1 expression on the cell surface (figure 1H). However, IFN-γ stimulation significantly increased the expression of PD-L1 on the surface of GL261 cells, with or without oncolytic virus infection (figure 1I). Given the potential role of PD-L1 in tumor immune evasion, it is crucial to study the expression of PD-L1 on the immune cells of the TME. Therefore, we next analyzed the expression of PD-L1 on myeloid cells, including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and macrophages. The results indicated that oncolytic adenovirus treatment increased both the percentage and mean fluorescence intensity of PD-L1+ myeloid cells, including PD-L1+ MDSCs and PD-L1+ macrophages (online supplemental figure 3A). In addition, we also found that the expression of PD-1 on the surface of tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes increased after i.t. injection of oncolytic adenoviruses (online supplemental figure 3B).

In summary, although the oncolytic adenovirus vaccine with PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein can efficiently provoke PEPvIII-specific T cell responses, the increased expression of PD-L1 in the TME caused by oncolytic adenovirus infection would engage with PD-1 on the surface of T cells, resulting in immunosuppression and may, in turn, weaken T cell responses mediated by the vaccine.

sec.title: Co-expression of GM-CSF and sPD-1 enhances the antiglioma activity of the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine in the syngeneic immunocompetent mouse models
sec.p: To reverse PD-1/PD-L1 mediated immunosuppression caused by the upregulated expression of PD-L1 in TME due to the oncolytic adenovirus infection, we attempted to co-express GM-CSF and sPD-1 in the E4 region of the oncolytic adenoviruses for therapeutic effects. To do so, the genes encoding the extracellular domains of murine PD-1 and murine GM-CSF were inserted into the E4 region of the plasmid pAd5-D24-HVR5-PEPvIII-Fiber-RGD. The resulting oncolytic adenovirus, named Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF, features a PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein and co-expresses murine GM-CSF and murine sPD-1 in the E4 region; we also refer to it as an "all-in-one" vaccine. Using a similar strategy, a control recombinant oncolytic adenovirus, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF, which expressed only murine GM-CSF, was also generated (figure 2A). All recombinant oncolytic adenoviruses were successfully generated with a titer of~1.0×1012 viral particles per milliliter. Online supplemental figure 4A shows representative images of the cytopathic effect of recombinant oncolytic adenoviruses. We confirmed that murine sPD-1 and murine GM-CSF could be secreted into the supernatant of the virus-infected GL261 cells (online supplemental figure 4B). Notably, the oncolytic activity of all the recombinant adenoviruses was not affected by the presence of any soluble proteins (online supplemental figure 4C,S1).

sec.p: Next, we used two intracranial glioma murine models to evaluate the antitumor activity of different types of oncolytic adenoviruses. In the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, tumor progression was monitored using luciferase-based imaging starting on day 14 post-implantation (figure 2B). Compared with the PBS-treated group, the Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-treated group moderately slowed tumor progression and prolonged median survival, with the median survival increasing from 30 days in the PBS group to 36 days (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII vs PBS, p<0.01) (figure 2B–D). Mice treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF exhibited significantly slower tumor progression and further extended median survival, with no significant difference between these two groups. Specifically, the median survival was 43 days for mice treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF vs PBS, p<0.001) and 47 days for those treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF vs PBS, p<0.001) (figure 2B–D). In the CT-2A/EGFRvIII murine model (imaging was initiated on day 12 post-implantation; figure 2E), trends similar to those in the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model were observed. Ad5-D24-PEPvIII modestly slowed tumor progression and prolonged median survival from 23 days (PBS group) to 30 days (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII vs PBS, p<0.05) (figure 2F,G). Both Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF also further slowed tumor progression and prolonged median survival to 38 and 40 days, respectively (p<0.001 for both vs PBS), without intergroup difference (figure 2G). In both orthotopic glioma murine models, treatment with Ad5-D24 resulted in a non-significant survival benefit compared with PBS (Ad5-D24 vs PBS, p=0.066 in the GL261/EGFRvIII model and Ad5-D24 vs PBS, p=0.142 in the CT-2A/EGFRvIII model) (figure 2D and G). To evaluate antitumor activity, histopathological changes were examined using H&E staining in both intracranial glioma models. In the treatment groups—particularly those receiving Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF—H&E staining revealed extensive tumor cell apoptosis or necrosis, with greater numbers and deeper infiltration of lymphocytes in both the central and peripheral tumor regions compared with PBS or other oncolytic adenovirus treatments (figure 2H). Immunohistochemical analysis of CD8+ T cell infiltration demonstrated that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF treatment significantly increased the numbers of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII treatment (figure 2I,J). These findings indicate that the oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine co-expressing murine GM-CSF and murine sPD-1 enhances CD8+ T cell infiltration into tumor tissues, thereby improving antitumor activity.

However, it remained unclear whether the enhancement of antitumor activity depends on the highly efficient antigen presentation mediated by hexon modification or is solely attributed to the immunomodulatory effects of GM-CSF and sPD-1. To validate the necessity and pivotal role of PEPvIII modification in enhancing the antitumor immune response and therapeutic efficacy, and to distinguish the independent contributions of tumor antigen presentation and immunomodulation, we generated an additional control adenovirus, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, which expresses murine GM-CSF and murine sPD-1 but lacks the PEPvIII modification in the hexon protein (figure 2A and online supplemental figure 5A). In vitro studies demonstrated that following the infection of GL261 cells with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, the secretion of murine GM-CSF and murine sPD-1 was detected in the cell culture supernatant (online supplemental figure 5B). Moreover, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF exhibited comparable oncolytic activity in multiple glioma cell lines (online supplemental figure 5C).

We then evaluated the antitumor effect of Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF in vivo. Compared with Ad5-D24 treatment, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF suppressed tumor growth and prolonged median survival in both orthotopic glioma murine models. Specifically, in the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, median survival was extended from 33 days (Ad5-D24 group) to 39 days (Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF vs Ad5-D24, p<0.01) (figure 2D). In the CT-2A/EGFRvIII model, median survival was prolonged from 28 days (Ad5-D24 group) to 33 days (Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF vs Ad5-D24, p<0.05) (figure 2G). This enhanced antitumor effect likely results from the combined immunomodulatory actions of GM-CSF and sPD-1, which synergistically augment the therapeutic efficacy of Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF. Despite their comparable in vitro tumor cell lysis capabilities, in vivo bioluminescence imaging demonstrated that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF achieved significantly greater antitumor efficacy than Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF in the CT-2A/EGFRvIII murine model, with median survival extended from 33 days (Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF group) to 40 days (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF vs Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, p<0.05) (figure 2E–G). In the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, in vivo bioluminescence imaging revealed no significant difference in short-term tumor suppression between Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF (figure 1B,C). However, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF significantly extended median survival compared with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF (Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF vs Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, p<0.05) (figure 2D). These findings indicate that the immunomodulatory actions of GM-CSF and sPD-1 enhance therapeutic efficacy by significantly extending survival in both glioma models, and that the PEPvIII modification of the hexon protein further amplifies this effect, particularly in the CT-2A/EGFRvIII model, thereby producing synergistic therapeutic benefits.

sec.title: Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF enhances PEPvIII-specific T cell responses by promoting immune cell activation
sec.p: To better understand the mechanisms underlying the antitumor effects of the “all-in-one” oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine and to further clarify how the PEPvIII modification of the hexon protein and the immune modulatory factors expressed in the E4 region enhance the tumor antigen-specific immune response, we characterized the types and functional states of immune cell populations recruited into tumors by various oncolytic adenovirus treatments. In two orthotopic glioma murine models, compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-injected mice, those treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF showed increased infiltration of T lymphocytes (CD45+/CD3+), including CD8+ T cells, at the tumor site (figure 3A). These tumor-infiltrating T lymphocytes also exhibited enhanced activation, as indicated by upregulated IFN-γ and TNF-α expression (figure 3B,C). Moreover, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF significantly reduced PD-1 and T cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain containing protein-3 (TIM-3) expression on CD8+ T cells compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII (figure 3D). Compared with Ad5-D24, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF treatment significantly increased both the number and functionality of tumor-infiltrating T cells in both models (figure 3A–C). Notably, in the CT-2A/EGFRvIII murine model, T lymphocyte infiltration was further augmented by Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF compared with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF (figure 3A). We also observed that the expression of GM-CSF alone or co-expression with sPD-1 in the E4 region significantly promoted the maturation of tumor-infiltrating dendritic cells, as demonstrated by increased numbers of activated dendritic cells and elevated CD86 and MHCII (major histocompatibility complex class II) expression (figure 3E and online supplemental figure 6). In the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, no significant differences in natural killer cell infiltration were observed among the different treatment groups (online supplemental figure 7). Next, we evaluated the antitumor activity of these immune cells isolated from the GL261/EGFRvIII and CT-2A/EGFRvIII models by measuring IFN-γ secretion following stimulation with tumor antigens. After intratumoral injection of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells showed increased proliferation and IFN-γ secretion in response to in vitro stimulation with PEPvIII-pulsed dendritic cells, compared with those from other oncolytic adenovirus groups (figure 3F and online supplemental figure 8). Consistent with these findings, CD8+ T cells from the tumors or spleens of mice treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF showed greater activity against EGFRvIII+ tumor cells than those from other oncolytic adenovirus monotherapy groups (figure 3G,H). Both Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF enhanced the splenocyte response to the PEPvIII peptide, with no significant difference between them (online supplemental figure 9). Although Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF partially increased T cell infiltration and function, its capacity to induce a tumor-specific immune response was substantially weaker than that of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-PD-1-GM-CSF. This limitation may be due to the absence of PEPvIII modification in Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, which primarily elicits antiviral immune responses rather than tumor-specific immunity. Consequently, although GM-CSF and sPD-1 can remodel the TME, the deficiency of tumor antigens in the TME impairs antigen presentation and fails to elicit an effective tumor-specific immune response. Conversely, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII can provide sufficient tumor antigens, yet it still fails to present them efficiently due to its inability to remodel the TME. This ultimately leads to a weakened tumor-specific immune response. Collectively, these results highlight that co-expression of GM-CSF and sPD-1 enhances lymphocyte recruitment, boosts T cell activation and proliferation, and promotes dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation. This synergistic interplay between effective antigen presentation and immunomodulation amplifies the PEPvIII-specific T cell response induced by the PEPvIII-modified oncolytic adenovirus, contributing to a stronger antitumor effect.

sec.p: Myeloid cells are the most important component of the GBM microenvironment; the state and function of myeloid cells are of great significance for GBM treatment.27 Given their critical role in tumor immunity, we evaluated the number, status, and cytokine secretion profiles of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells in GL261/EGFRvIII glioma-bearing mice. We observed an increase in the numbers of MDSCs and macrophages infiltrating the tumors following treatment with various oncolytic adenoviruses compared with the PBS-treated group (figure 4A). Compared with the Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF group, MDSC infiltration was reduced after Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF treatment. No significant differences were observed in the numbers of tumor-infiltrating macrophages and MDSCs between the Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF groups. Immunohistochemical analysis showed that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF further increased CD68-labeled tumor-infiltrating macrophages and inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-positive cells, indicating M1-polarized macrophages (figure 4B–D). Flow cytometry further demonstrated that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF significantly enhanced TNF-α and IL-12 secretion by myeloid cells, while concomitantly reducing the secretion of IL-10, an immunosuppressive cytokine. IL-12 secretion by dendritic cells was also increased (figure 4E). In comparison with Ad5-D24, Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF more potently promoted myeloid cell activation (figure 4E). We also compared PD-L1 expression on myeloid cells after treatment with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF. Compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF, intratumoral injection of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF reduced PD-L1 expression on myeloid cells and decreased the proportion of PD-L1+ myeloid cells, including PD-L1+ MDSCs (figure 4F). Collectively, these data demonstrate that while an oncolytic adenovirus vaccine expressing GM-CSF and sPD-1 alone can partially reprogram myeloid cells, the PEPvIII modification of the hexon protein remains indispensable for maximizing immunomodulatory efficacy. This reprogramming, combined with efficient tumor antigen presentation, significantly promotes the secretion of immunomodulatory factors, enhances myeloid cell activation, alleviates immunosuppression, and fully activates the antitumor immune response. Furthermore, the co-expression of GM-CSF and sPD-1 may stimulate other immune cells to exert regulatory functions and indirectly modulate PD-L1 expression on myeloid cells, contributing to a more favorable immune environment for antitumor activity.

sec.title: Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF combined with PD-L1 blockade prolongs the survival of glioma-bearing mice by remodeling the immunosuppressive TME
sec.p: Our results above indicated that the “all-in-one” vaccine strategy enhanced tumor antigen-specific T cell responses by ameliorating the suppression of immune cells. However, it did not show an evident advantage in tumor treatment compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF, likely due to the inefficient blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 axis by sPD-1. Given the success of immune checkpoint inhibitors in tumor therapy, we next attempted to combine the vaccine with a PD-L1 inhibitor to enhance tumor treatment efficacy. We compared the therapeutic efficacy of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy with that of a combination treatment consisting of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and an anti-PD-L1 antibody in two syngeneic orthotopic glioma murine models. In the combination treatment group, four intraperitoneal doses of the anti-PD-L1 antibody were administered (figure 5A). In the orthotopic GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, the combination therapy exhibited a trend toward further suppressing glioma growth compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy (figure 5B,C). The combination therapy prolonged survival beyond 60 days in 62.5% of mice, whereas three injections of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF alone led to survival beyond 60 days in only 37.5% (figure 5D). When using the same combination treatment regimen as in the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model, 50% of CT-2A/EGFRvIII-bearing mice survived beyond 60 days, in contrast to only 12.5% survival observed with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy (figure 5E,F). H&E staining and immunohistochemistry analyses showed that, compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF alone, the combination treatment resulted in broader tumor necrotic areas and greater CD8+ T cell infiltration (figure 5G–I). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the PEPvIII-modified oncolytic adenovirus vaccine achieves optimal therapeutic efficacy when combined with GM-CSF and PD-L1 blockade.

sec.p: To investigate the mechanism underlying this enhanced effect, we performed comparative immune profiling of the TME in both orthotopically implanted GL261/EGFRvIII and CT-2A/EGFRvIII syngeneic C57BL/6 murine models. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that both Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy and combination therapy significantly increased the recruitment of T lymphocytes and activated dendritic cells compared with PBS treatment (figure 6A and C). Notably, the combination therapy showed the highest recruitment of these immune cells among the treatment groups. However, no statistically significant differences were observed between combination therapy and monotherapy in T cell activation, MDSC infiltration, or infiltration of M1-like proinflammatory macrophages (figure 6B, D and E). We further analyzed PD-L1 expression and the percentage of PD-L1+ myeloid cells isolated from GL261/EGFRvIII tumors following each treatment. As shown in figure 6F, combination therapy significantly reduced PD-L1 expression on these cells and decreased the infiltration of PD-L1+ myeloid cells, including PD-L1+ MDSCs and PD-L1+ dendritic cells. Compared with other treatment groups, combination therapy also significantly reduced the infiltration of regulatory T cells (Tregs) (figure 6G). Together, these findings suggest that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF combined with PD-L1 blockade enhances immune cell infiltration and significantly reduces PD-L1 expression on immune cells. This effect may disrupt the immunosuppressive microenvironment and shift it toward a more immunostimulatory state, thereby contributing to stronger therapeutic efficacy.

sec.title: The combination of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and PD-L1 blockade enhances the T cell responses against PEPvIII peptide and tumor neoantigens
sec.p: To determine whether combining the oncolytic vaccine with PD-L1 blockade could enhance T cell-specific responses to tumor antigens, we isolated tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells after combination treatment and measured IFN-γ secretion following a 40-hour co-culture with primary astrocytes, GL261 cells, or GL261/EGFRvIII cells. As shown in figure 7A, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells from the combination treatment group exhibited significantly increased IFN-γ release when co-cultured with GL261 or GL261/EGFRvIII cells compared with cells from mice that received intratumoral injections of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF alone. This effect was most pronounced in co-cultures with GL261/EGFRvIII cells (figure 7A). Similarly, splenic CD8+ T cells from combination-treated mice secreted significantly higher levels of IFN-γ when co-cultured with GL261/EGFRvIII cells (online supplemental figure 10). Furthermore, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells isolated from combination-treated mice bearing GL261/EGFRvIII tumors showed greater activity against mouse dendritic cells pulsed with the PEPvIII peptide than did those from mice treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF alone (figure 7B). In CT-2A/EGFRvIII glioma-bearing mice, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and splenocytes from the combination treatment group also showed the highest IFN-γ secretion when stimulated with tumor antigens (figure 7C,D). Following oncolytic adenovirus treatment, tumor neoantigens are typically released. To test whether different treatments could induce neoantigen-specific T cell responses, we focused on GARC-1, an H-2Db-restricted, GL261-derived immunodominant neoantigen recognized by T cells in C57BL/6J mice.28 29 We isolated tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells from each treatment group and co-incubated them with mouse dendritic cells primed with varying concentrations of the GARC-1 peptide. As shown in figure 7E, tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells from GL261/EGFRvIII tumor-bearing mice that received the combination treatment exhibited the greatest activity against dendritic cells pulsed with GARC-1 at all tested concentrations and secreted the highest levels of IFN-γ compared with T cells from other treatment groups. Consistently, splenocytes from the combination treatment group showed the strongest response to GARC-1, even at a low peptide concentration (10 µg/mL) (figure 7F). Notably, compared with mice treated with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, both tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and splenocytes from Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF-treated mice showed significantly enhanced activity against the GARC-1 peptide (figure 7E,F). These findings suggest that intratumoral administration of Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF combined with PD-L1 blockade can more effectively activate T cell responses to the PEPvIII peptide and tumor neoantigen epitopes than Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy. This combination strategy may help overcome the limited therapeutic effects of the vaccine associated with a low mutation burden and tumor heterogeneity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Currently, five main immunotherapeutic approaches are considered for treating GBM: (1) immune checkpoint inhibitors30; (2) Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) -T cell therapy31; (3) oncolytic viruses32; (4) cancer vaccines33 34 and (5) cytokine therapy,35 among which, cancer vaccine-based immunotherapy provides a promising option for patients with GBM. However, there are many obstacles in the development of vaccine-based GBM immunotherapy, including low tumor mutation burden, immunosuppressive TME, poor T cell infiltration, and impaired antigen processing and presentation pathways. To date, only a few vaccination strategies have reached phase III clinical testing in patients with GBM, whereas numerous others are in the earlier stages of clinical development.36 Therefore, optimizing vaccine design, including personalized antigen selection, multi-antigen targeting, and improving vaccine platforms or adjuvants, can be important strategies for eradicating GBM in the future.

This dual mechanism of action—the direct killing of tumor cells and the elicitation of antitumor immunity—endows oncolytic virus-based tumor vaccines with obvious advantages over traditional tumor vaccines, such as peptide vaccines and dendritic cell vaccines. In an adenovirus particle, there are typically 240 copies of hexon protein. Here, to maximally present the number of PEPvIII in oncolytic adenovirus particles, we modified the hexon protein of Delta-24-RGD oncolytic adenovirus vector with PEPvIII. In two orthotopic glioma murine models, the experimental results showed that compared with the PBS group, after treatment with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII, the number and activity of infiltrating T lymphocytes, including CD8+ and CD4+ T cells within the tumors, significantly increased, and the median survival of mice was prolonged. ELISA analysis revealed that tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells isolated from Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-treated mice secreted higher levels of IFN-γ on co-culture with EGFRvIII-overexpressing tumor cells or with PEPvIII-pulsed dendritic cells than those from Ad5-D24-treated mice. No significant difference was observed when these cells were co-cultured with GL261 cells, CT-2A cells, or astrocytes, suggesting that the oncolytic adenovirus with PEPvIII-modified hexon protein was capable of eliciting specific immune responses to EGFRvIII antigens, as well as to PEPvIII peptides. These results are exciting since activating tumor-specific T cell immune responses is crucial for improving the efficacy of vaccine therapy. To further improve the presentation of PEPvIII or other tumor antigens by antigen-presenting cells, we also constructed an oncolytic adenovirus expressing GM-CSF in the E4 region. GM-CSF is a powerful stimulator of antigen-presenting cells and is crucial for the development and maturation of dendritic cells, which in turn enhances T cell activation.14 37 Previous studies have shown that GM-CSF can induce antitumor immunity through various administration routes.38 39 Here, the oncolytic adenovirus carrying GM-CSF strengthened the recruitment of T cells, promoted the infiltration and maturation of dendritic cells, and further enhanced antitumor activity, emphasizing the importance of the oncolytic adenovirus delivering GM-CSF.

Consistent with previous studies,26 40 our oncolytic adenovirus vaccine recruited effector T cells and induced pro-inflammatory responses, leading to increased release of IFN-γ and TNF-α, resulting in upregulation of PD-L1 expression in the TME. The PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway can drive T cells toward a dysfunctional state, which impairs anti-tumor immune responses. For instance, the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway promotes the polarization of macrophages to the M2 phenotype and supports immunosuppression by secreting immunosuppressive cytokines and reducing their phagocytic killing abilities.41 Peng et al reported that the expression of PD-L1 on dendritic cells attenuates T cell activation.42 Thus, the PD-1/PD-L1 axis is one of the main molecular signaling pathways constituting the immunosuppressive TME of GBM. Therefore, blocking the interaction between PD-L1 and PD-1 is of great significance for improving immune cell function. As a soluble form of PD-1, sPD-1 can bind to PD-L1 expressed by many cells and block the interaction of three PD-1/PD-L1 pathways: PD-L1/CD80, PD-1/PD-L1, and PD-1/PD-L2.43 Many studies have shown that sPD-1 can regulate immune responses, enhance the function of CD8+ T cells, and improve antitumor activity.44 45 Therefore, sPD-1 is considered to have potential in cancer immune checkpoint inhibition therapies. In this study, to alleviate PD-L1-mediated immunosuppression, we first adopted the strategy of inserting the sPD-1 gene into the E4 region of oncolytic adenovirus carrying PEPvIII and GM-CSF. Our results indicated that sPD-1 expression not only further enhanced the activity and proliferation of PEPvIII specific-T cells and reversed the exhausted phenotype of T cells, but also activated tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells. This activation included promoting dendritic cell maturation and M1-like macrophage infiltration, reducing MDSC infiltration, upregulating the secretion of the immune-activating cytokines TNF-α and IL-12, and downregulating the secretion of the immunosuppressive factor IL-10. Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF therapy also enhanced the specific immune response of tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells and splenocytes to EGFRvIII antigens and PEPvIII peptides.

To further dissect the independent contributions of tumor antigen presentation and immunomodulatory factor expression, we generated Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF, a control adenovirus co-expressing GM-CSF and sPD-1 but lacking PEPvIII modification on the hexon protein. Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF demonstrated comparable in vitro oncolytic activity to Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF. However, in vivo bioluminescence imaging revealed that Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF in the CT-2A/EGFRvIII murine model, whereas both adenoviruses exhibited comparable short-term tumor suppression in the GL261/EGFRvIII murine model. This finding suggests that, owing to the inherently high immunogenicity of the GL261 model, the immunostimulatory effects of GM-CSF and sPD-1 alone were sufficient to achieve an initial suppression of tumor growth, even without the PEPvIII-mediated enhancement of tumor antigen presentation. Nevertheless, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF treatment further prolonged the median survival of mice compared with Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF in both glioma murine models. This survival benefit is likely attributed to enhanced tumor-specific T cell responses mediated by PEPvIII modification, as supported by ELISA results showing that T cell responses against EGFRvIII+ tumor cells and PEPvIII peptide were significantly weaker in adenoviruses lacking the PEPvIII modification than in their PEPvIII-modified counterparts. Collectively, these results demonstrate that although immunoadjuvants such as GM-CSF and sPD-1 can remodel the TME, sufficient tumor antigen presentation remains essential for priming effective antitumor immunity, highlighting its importance in developing immunotherapies for poorly immunogenic malignancies. Ad5-D24-PEPvIII can successfully induce initial activation of PEPvIII-specific T cells by displaying high-copy PEPvIII in the hexon protein, but it elicits only transient effector T cell responses due to its inability to overcome the immunosuppressive TME. In contrast, Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF not only continuously presents high-density antigens to dendritic cells via the PEPvIII-modified hexon protein but also effectively mitigates the immunosuppressive state within the TME. This strategy, which integrates efficient tumor antigen presentation with immunomodulation, generates a synergistic effect that enhances T cell effector function and amplifies the tumor antigen-specific immune response. Importantly, the comparative analysis of Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF and Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF also informs future vaccine design. The results support the rationale for “all-in-one” vaccine vectors that co-deliver tumor antigens and immunomodulators.

However, although the analysis of TME cell components showed that the co-expression of sPD-1 and GM-CSF was effective in reversing immune silencing, the median survival of mice treated with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF was not significantly prolonged compared with the Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF-treated group. We speculated that this may be related to the low concentration of sPD-1 secreted within the TME. In addition, as the virus colonizes the tumor, the host’s antiviral immunity is activated and mobilized to limit the replication and spread of the virus, ultimately leading to its clearance, which limits the persistent expression of sPD-1.46 In future studies, we could further optimize our experimental design by, for example, fusing sPD-1 with the Fc fragment of immunoglobulin. This approach leverages the natural structure of immunoglobulins to prolong the half-life and enhance the stability of sPD-1. In addition, we could enhance the secretion of sPD-1 by using an appropriate secretion signal peptide and a strong promoter. These strategies may enhance the sustained expression and function of sPD-1, thereby maximizing its ability to block PD-1/PD-L1 signaling and reverse T cell exhaustion.

Numerous studies have shown that combining oncolytic viruses with PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors can not only synergistically activate the immune system and enhance the antitumor immune response, but also overcome tumor resistance to these inhibitors.13 47 48 Therefore, we then attempted to administer Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF in combination with an anti-PD-L1 antibody for treatment and compared it with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy. We observed that in both glioma murine models, combination treatment with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-GM-CSF and the anti-PD-L1 antibody further increased survival compared with Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy. Moreover, combination treatment reduced PD-L1 expression and the percentage of PD-L1+ myeloid cells. The percentage of Treg cell infiltration was also reduced. These results indicated that combination therapy further reversed the functional suppression of T cells caused by PD-L1+ myeloid cells, enhanced tumor antigen-specific CD8+ T cell activity, and significantly prolonged the survival of tumor-bearing mice. Importantly, the combination of the novel oncolytic adenovirus vaccine with PD-L1 blockade not only significantly enhanced responses against the tumor antigens but also synergistically boosted T cell responses against the tumor neoantigen GARC-1. The results suggest that the combination therapy may help overcome the limitations of single-peptide vaccines, such as low mutation burden and antigen loss, which are common challenges in GBM treatment. Although Ad5-D24-PEPvIII-sPD-1-GM-CSF monotherapy induces a weaker GARC-1-specific immune response compared with the combination therapy, it elicits significantly stronger responses than either Ad5-D24-sPD-1-GM-CSF or Ad5-D24-PEPvIII monotherapy. These findings further highlight the superiority of the “all-in-one” vaccine design in enhancing antitumor immunity.

In summary, we constructed a novel oncolytic adenovirus-based PEPvIII vaccine by modifying the hexon protein with PEPvIII. When this vaccine is combined with the adjuvant function of GM-CSF and blockade of the PD-1/PD-L1 axis, it can maximally enhance T cell-specific responses against PEPvIII and tumor neoantigens, and greatly improve the therapeutic efficacy of the vaccine. Our research overcomes the shortcomings of traditional peptide-based vaccines and provides a more effective, individualized treatment for patients with tumors.
